opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key difference is where you start from. With the old game-playing systems, something like AlphaZero, you were starting from a randomly initialized network. The agent knows nothing, so the early part of the RL curve is spent just discovering the basic structure of the game, and you need an enormous number of episodes before you get any useful reward signal at all. Those curves look pretty brutal: lots of compute for not much progress, and then eventually things take off.

With language models, you're starting from a pretrained model that has already absorbed a huge amount of human knowledge. It already knows how to reason a bit, how to write code, how to use tools to some extent. So from the very first step of RL you're getting meaningful reward signal. The model can actually solve some fraction of the tasks you give it, and RL is really about sharpening and reinforcing behaviors that already exist in the distribution rather than discovering them from scratch. That's why you see these really steep early gains with comparatively little compute.

The interesting open question is what happens further along the curve. One view is that RL on language models mostly elicits capabilities that were latent in pretraining, so you'd expect it to saturate at some point. The other view, which I lean towards, is that if you give the model sufficiently hard tasks with clean, verifiable rewards, and enough compute, it can genuinely learn new things beyond what was in the pretraining data, much like AlphaGo eventually went beyond human play. The difference is that we're getting to skip that painful cold-start phase. So the real bottleneck shifts from "can we get any signal at all" to "can we build environments and reward signals that are rich and hard enough to keep pushing the model forward."

r001.rationale: The response contrasts cold-start game agents with language models that can solve some tasks immediately, but it does not say that one player always wins and supplies the game reward signal.

r002.rationale: It attributes steep early RL gains to pretrained models already knowing how to reason, code, and use tools, which lets them solve some tasks from the start.

r003.rationale: It says RL can reinforce or elicit capabilities latent in pretraining, but does not explain apparent learning from one example.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people miss is that the game-playing curves were always measuring the wrong thing, or at least a thing that doesn't transfer. With AlphaGo or AlphaZero, you had this beautifully clean setup: perfect simulator, dense and unambiguous reward, you can generate essentially infinite data for free, and the policy starts from zero. So the curve you get is mostly a story about compute and search. It goes up, it saturates at superhuman, and then it just stops meaning anything because there's nowhere left to go in that one environment.

Language models start from the opposite end. The pretrained model already has this enormous prior over how the world works, so RL isn't teaching it the game from scratch, it's more like sharpening a capability that's latently already there. That changes the shape of the curve in a few ways. One, you get a lot of the gain very quickly, because you're mostly selecting among behaviours the model could already do and reinforcing the ones that actually work. Two, the ceiling isn't defined by one environment. If you RL a model on math and it gets better at writing code or at structuring a long chain of reasoning, that's generalization you basically never saw in the game systems. The thing you're measuring is how much the model's general reasoning improves, not how good it got at Go.

The harder part, and I think this is where the real difference shows up, is the reward. In games the reward is given to you. In language it's the whole problem. For anything with a verifiable answer, math, code with tests, you can make the loop reasonably tight and the curves actually look a bit like the game curves, pretty steady improvement as you scale environment compute. For anything fuzzy you're training against a learned reward model or a rubric, and the curve becomes as much about the quality and robustness of that signal as it is about the policy. You can get the policy climbing happily on your metric while it's exploiting some quirk of the grader. So I'd say the game curves were compute-limited and the language model curves are much more environment- and reward-limited. The interesting question for the next few years is how fast we can build out that supply of good environments, because that, more than algorithmic cleverness, is what sets the slope.

r001.rationale: The response says game rewards are directly provided while language-model rewards are harder to obtain, but it does not communicate that one player always wins.

r002.rationale: It links rapid early RL gains to the pretrained model already having relevant capabilities, which RL then sharpens.

r003.rationale: It describes reinforcing behaviors the model could already perform, but does not address apparent learning from one example.

astra-6.text:
The big difference is where you’re starting from. With something like AlphaZero, you start with a randomly initialized network, and reinforcement learning has to build essentially the whole capability. With a language model, you’ve already spent an enormous amount of compute on pretraining. Before you do any RL, it can already write code, explain mathematics, and produce at least plausible attempts at very difficult problems.

So an early RL curve can be a little deceptive. Are you teaching the model something new, or are you making it reliably do something it could already do occasionally? If it solves a problem one time in a hundred, there’s a lot of room to improve by reinforcing those successful trajectories. That’s useful, but it doesn’t by itself tell you how far the process can ultimately go.

The other difference is that games give you this incredibly clean training environment. You have a definite win condition, you can generate more experience, and with self-play your opponent improves alongside you. For language models, constructing a comparable distribution of tasks—with reliable rewards and a difficulty level that keeps advancing—is much more of the problem.

So I wouldn’t look at a language-model RL curve flattening and immediately conclude that reinforcement learning has hit a fundamental limit. It could mean you’ve exhausted what that particular task distribution and reward signal can teach you. The interesting question is whether you can keep expanding the training environment so that more compute continues to produce new capabilities.

r001.rationale: It contrasts games’ definite win conditions and reliable rewards with the difficulty of obtaining reliable language-model rewards, but does not communicate that a player always wins in the game setting.

r002.rationale: It says pretraining gives language models substantial capabilities before RL, but does not state that this explains the absence of an initial flat phase in RL curves.

r003.rationale: It explains that reinforcing a successful trajectory can make a model reliably do something it could already do occasionally, using a problem it solves one time in a hundred as an example.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is what the starting point represents. With a game-playing system, you can start with a policy that’s essentially random and watch reinforcement learning build up the ability to play the game. The learning curve captures a huge amount of capability acquisition.

With a language model, you’re starting from a pretrained model that already has a vast repertoire of behaviors. It can often produce a correct solution, but it doesn’t reliably choose to. So an improvement from reinforcement learning could mean that it’s learning something new, or that it’s getting better at selecting and composing things it already knows. The curve alone doesn’t tell you which.

There’s also a difference in the environment. In a game, you have a clear reward, and self-play can keep generating harder opponents. For language models, the tasks you train on and what you can reliably score become much more consequential. Getting better at your training reward isn’t automatically the same as getting broadly more capable.

So I’d be cautious about putting the curves next to each other and extrapolating. You’d want to know how performance changes with more training compute, but also whether the gains transfer to new problems and whether the model is finding solutions that the starting model couldn’t find even with lots of attempts.

r001.rationale: It contrasts clear game rewards with language-model scoring, but does not state that one player always wins in the games or that language-model rewards depend on sometimes succeeding.

r002.rationale: It says pretrained models already have a broad repertoire, but does not connect that to the absence of an initial flat phase in reinforcement-learning curves.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning may improve selection or composition of known capabilities, but does not explain apparent learning from one example as eliciting capabilities supported by pretraining.
